title: Flexible Intensities Matter: A comprehensive re-evaluation of Hawkes Processes and Neural Temporal Point Processes
claim: Additive, interpretable kernel-sum intensity models differ from encoder-plus-head models that map history to a flexible, non-additive intensity.
layout: 2 stacked panels sharing a time axis, bottom-up flow, dashed query line
description: The figure stacks two panels on a shared time axis. The visible top strip is the end of the Hawkes panel: blue and red kernel curves rise from event markers and decay to the right, labeled φ_{d_i→d}(t−t_i). The bottom panel is headed "2. Neural TPP". A time axis holds alternating blue circles and red triangles for the two event types. Gray arrows fan from each event to a gray "Neural Encoder" box, which outputs hidden states h_t1 to h_tN. Those feed a "Head: f(t, h_t)" box. Dashed vertical arrows go up to a dark purple piecewise intensity curve λ*_d(t), with open circles at jumps. A dashed vertical line marks the query time t > t_N, splitting "observed history" from "future". A boxed formula defines λ*_d(t′) = f(t′, h_ti). The eye goes first to the purple curve and the encoder boxes.
caption: Conceptual comparison of Hawkes processes (1) and neural TPPs (2), illustrated on an event sequence with two event types (• type A, ▲type B). Top (Hawkes process). Each past event interacts via a kernel response ϕdi→d(t −ti) (colored curves) on top of a (possibly time-varying) baseline µd(t) (thin solid line). The total intensity (upper sub-panel) is the sum of baseline and active kernels. At any query time t, the intensity is thus the baseline plus the sum of kernel contributions from all past events. Bottom (Neural TPP). A neural encoder processes the same event history and outputs a hidden state at each event location. The head of the neural TPP projects this encoding to an intensity function. Conceptually, this lets neural TPPs capture higher-order, non-additive interactions between events, at the cost of the interpretable decomposition of the Hawkes process.
abstract: Temporal point processes (TPPs) are the canonical model class for event sequences in continuous time, with applications ranging from seismology to electronic health records. Recent benchmarks report that neural TPPs substantially outperform their classical counterparts, such as Hawkes processes. However, these comparisons set flexible neural models against Hawkes processes in their most restricted forms and covered only a narrow range of domains. We revisit this comparison under autoregressive next-event prediction, evaluating Poisson and Hawkes processes of increasing flexibility against neural TPPs on five established benchmarks and two large-scale medical tasks derived from UK Biobank disease histories and MIMIC-IV ICU records. First, once Hawkes processes are equipped with flexible, learnable baselines and kernels, the previously reported gap to neural TPPs largely closes. Second, neural TPPs are likewise limited by their intensity parametrization: a Transformer with a spline-based intensity head outperforms previous intensity-based neural TPPs and matches or exceeds the intensity-free model. Decomposing the log-likelihood into time and type terms shows that this gain lies almost entirely in modeling when events occur (log p(t)) rather than which type occurs (log p(d|t)). Third, only on MIMIC-IV do neural TPPs retain an advantage in predicting event types, underscoring the value of complex datasets for evaluating TPPs. We release TorchPP, an open-source PyTorch framework with unified implementations of classical and neural TPPs.
